provenance: Shimomura Kanzan (leading Nihonga painter, 1873–1930) | Azabu Museum of Art | Christie's, New York, Japanese Screens, Paintings and Prints, 27 October 1998, Lot 243 | | Published | Gotō Shigeki ed., Ukiyo-e taikei, vol. 6, Utamaro, Eishi, Tokyo, Shūeisha, 1973, pl. 63 and p. 131 | | For this signature and seal, compare in particular the hanging scroll by Eishi Ensō kyūbijinzu (Heads of Nine Beauties in a Roundel) in the MOA Museum of Art, Atami; see www.moaart.or.jp/collections/079/; also reproduced in colour in William Watson ed., The Great Japan Exhibition: Art of the Edo Period 1600–1868, exhibition catalogue, Royal Academy of Arts, London, 24 October 1981–21 February 1982, cat. no. 64a (p. 182). | | When this painting was once remounted, it was discovered that parts of the garments had been painted on the reverse of the silk as well as the front (a technique known as urazaishiki) perhaps in order to emulate the depth of colour achieved by repeated applications of pigment in woodblock prints of the same era. provenance: Richard Kruml, London, 1986 | | In the Noh drama Matsukaze—as well as the later kabuki play Shiokumi (The Salt Gatherers)—the Heian-period courtier Ariwara no Yukihira is exiled to Suma, where he befriends the two sisters. When he returns to the capital, he gives them his jacket and hat as tokens of his affection. Here the beautiful women set their buckets down under a pine tree and, longing for their beloved, put on his garments. | | For a closely related painting by the same artist, compare Museum of Fine Arts, Boston, https://collections.mfa.org/objects/26624/parodies-of-historical-figure-subjects-of-china-and-japan?ctx=27742ee8-af28-41c0-9edd-4b86ce59f902&idx=6; and see Anne Nishimura Morse ed., Drama and Desire: Japanese Paintings from the Floating World, 1690–1850, exhibition catalogue, Japan/USA/Canada, 2006–2008, Boston, MFA Publications, 2007, cat. no. 21. The 'slender, willowy figure style' favoured by Kawamata Tsunemasa, a little-known artist who specialized in painting beautiful women, would later be adopted by the much more famous Suzuki Harunobu. For another work by the artist in the Roger Weston Collection, see Janice Katz and Mami Hatayama eds., Painting the Floating World: Ukiyo-e Masterpieces from the Weston Collection, exhibition catalogue, The Art Institute of Chicago, 2018, cat. no. 42.

A high-born loyal servant of the Mito branch of Japan's ruling Tokugawa family, Tachihara Kyōsho studied painting from an early age and became a pupil of Tani Bunchō in 1812. He interacted with many other artists including Tsubaki Chinzan, Takaku Aigai, and Watanabe Kazan; viewed and copied historic Chinese paintings, especially those by Yun Shouping and Shen Nanpin; and compiled several scholarly works including Kinsei shoga nenpyō (A Chronological Table of Modern Calligraphy and Painting). His painting of a grapevine (Tokyo National Museum, 1836), executed in similarly vigorous and fluid brushwork to the present Lot, is registered as a Jūyō Bunkazai (Important Cultural Property, see www.tnm.jp/modules/r_collection/index.php?controller=dtl&colid=A12101). | | This lot contains ivory and has been registered in accordance with the Ivory Act (Section 10), Ref. 4WQUM8KU.
